outcomes.title: Rooms and places in a house
outcomes.objective: Name the kitchen, bedroom, bathroom and garden and say what we do in each place.
prerequisites: Knows the words house and bed

misconceptions.description: Uses the general word room or house instead of the specific word

teachingSuccessCriteria: Matches each place to its use
Uses the correct place word in a sentence

lesson.title: Places in my home
lesson.objective: Name the kitchen, bedroom, bathroom and garden and say what we do in each place.

objectives: Name the kitchen, bedroom, bathroom and garden and say what we do in each place.
successCriteria: Matches each place to its use
Uses the correct place word in a sentence
examples: I cook dinner in the kitchen.
My bed is in the bedroom.
We wash our hands in the bathroom.
There is a tree in the garden.

outcomes.studyNotes: A house has many places. The kitchen is the room where we cook food. The bedroom is the room with your bed. The bathroom is the room where we wash. The garden is outside the house, with trees. Use in the: I cook in the kitchen. Do not say "the room" when you can use a clear word like kitchen or bathroom.

scriptedTutor.explanation: A house has different places. We cook in the kitchen, we keep our bed in the bedroom, we wash in the bathroom, and the garden is outside.
hints: Think: what do you do in this place?
The bedroom has a bed. The bathroom is for washing.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Think about the meaning and try again.
scriptedTutor.closing: Well done. You know four places in a house.

outcomes.title: Opposites: hot/cold, early/late, cheap/expensive, easy/difficult
outcomes.objective: Give the opposite of common adjectives and use opposites in sentences.
prerequisites: Knows basic adjectives like big and small

misconceptions.description: Makes an opposite by adding not or un- to the word
Gives a related word instead of the opposite

teachingSuccessCriteria: Uses the opposite in a sentence

lesson.title: Opposite words
lesson.objective: Give the opposite of common adjectives and use opposites in sentences.

objectives: Give the opposite of common adjectives and use opposites in sentences.
successCriteria: Uses the opposite in a sentence
examples: Tea is hot but juice is cold.
The bus was early, but the train was late.
This bag is cheap, but that watch is expensive.
The first question is easy, but the last is difficult.

outcomes.studyNotes: Opposites are words with a different meaning: hot and cold, early and late, cheap and expensive, easy and difficult. Learn them in pairs. We do not make these opposites with un- or not. We use a different word: the opposite of late is early, not unlate. Use the right opposite to say the other idea clearly.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Opposites are word pairs: hot and cold, early and late, cheap and expensive, easy and difficult. Each opposite is a different word.
hints: Which word has the other meaning?
Do not add un- or not. Use a new word.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Think about the meaning and try again.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. Learn opposites in pairs.

outcomes.title: Job words with -er and -or
outcomes.objective: Turn verbs into person nouns with -er or -or (for example teach to teacher).
prerequisites: Knows common verbs such as teach and drive

misconceptions.description: Adds -er to a word that already ends in e

teachingSuccessCriteria: Adds -er (or -r after e) to name a person who does the action
Uses -or on words like actor and visitor

lesson.title: Who does the action?
lesson.objective: Turn verbs into person nouns with -er or -or (for example teach to teacher).

objectives: Turn verbs into person nouns with -er or -or (for example teach to teacher).
successCriteria: Adds -er (or -r after e) to name a person who does the action
Uses -or on words like actor and visitor
examples: My aunt is a teacher.
A bus driver stops here.
The actor is in a new film.
Each visitor signs a book.

outcomes.studyNotes: To name the person who does an action, add -er to the verb: teach becomes teacher. If the verb already ends in e, add only -r: drive becomes driver, not driveer. Some words end in -or instead: act becomes actor and visit becomes visitor. You must learn which words take -or. If the verb is short with one vowel and one consonant, double the consonant.

scriptedTutor.explanation: A person who does an action is often named with -er: teacher. After e we add only r: driver. Some words use -or: actor, visitor.
hints: Does the verb end in e?
Some words need -or. Try to remember which.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Think about the meaning and try again.
scriptedTutor.closing: Well done. You can make person words.

outcomes.title: Collocations with make and do
outcomes.objective: Choose make or do correctly with common nouns (do homework, make a mistake).
prerequisites: Knows the verbs make and do

misconceptions.description: Uses do for things we create or produce
Uses make for tasks and chores

teachingSuccessCriteria: Uses do with tasks and duties
Uses make with things we produce or decide

lesson.title: Make or do?
lesson.objective: Choose make or do correctly with common nouns (do homework, make a mistake).

objectives: Choose make or do correctly with common nouns (do homework, make a mistake).
successCriteria: Uses do with tasks and duties
Uses make with things we produce or decide
examples: I do my homework after school.
Dad does the dishes every night.
Everyone can make a mistake.
I need to make a phone call.

items.prompt: Complete with make or do: "I ___ my homework at six."
Complete with make or do: "Sorry, I ___ a mistake."

outcomes.studyNotes: Make and do are often confused. We use do for tasks, jobs and duties: do homework, do the dishes. We use make when we create or produce something, or for some actions: make a mistake, make a phone call. These pairs are fixed. We say do homework, not make homework. We say make a mistake, not do a mistake. Learn each phrase as a whole.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Use do for tasks and duties (do homework, do the dishes). Use make for creating something or fixed actions (make a mistake, make a phone call).
hints: Is it a task or something you create?
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Think about the meaning and try again.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. Learn each phrase as a whole.

outcomes.title: Phrasal verbs: look after, give up, put off, turn down
outcomes.objective: Use four common phrasal verbs with the correct particle and meaning.
prerequisites: Knows the verbs look, give, put and turn

misconceptions.description: Uses the wrong particle, so the meaning changes
Uses the verb alone and drops the particle

teachingSuccessCriteria: Chooses the phrasal verb with the right meaning
Uses the correct particle and tense form

lesson.title: Everyday phrasal verbs
lesson.objective: Use four common phrasal verbs with the correct particle and meaning.

objectives: Use four common phrasal verbs with the correct particle and meaning.
successCriteria: Chooses the phrasal verb with the right meaning
Uses the correct particle and tense form
examples: Please look after my dog this weekend.
He decided to give up chocolate.
Do not put off your work.
Can you turn down the TV?

items.prompt: Complete with a phrasal verb: "I will ___ the party until next month." (postpone)

outcomes.studyNotes: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word, and it has its own meaning. Look after means take care of. Give up means stop trying or stop a habit. Put off means do something later. Turn down means make quieter, or say no to an offer. If you change the particle, the meaning changes: turn up is different from turn down. Never drop the particle: give up, not just give. Learn each phrasal verb as one unit.

scriptedTutor.explanation: A phrasal verb has a verb and a particle. Look after is take care of, give up is stop, put off is delay, turn down is refuse or make quieter.
hints: Keep both words of the phrasal verb.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Think about the meaning and try again.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. Remember each phrasal verb has its own meaning.

outcomes.title: Confusable words: library, bookshop, actually, currently
outcomes.objective: Avoid common mix-ups for Arabic speakers: library vs bookshop and actually vs currently.
prerequisites: Knows the words book, shop and now

misconceptions.description: Treats library and bookshop as the same word (one Arabic word covers both)
misconceptions.exampleWrong: I want to buy a book at the library.
I am actually living in Cairo.

teachingSuccessCriteria: Uses library for borrowing and bookshop for buying
Uses currently for now and actually for in fact

lesson.title: Words that look or feel the same
lesson.objective: Avoid common mix-ups for Arabic speakers: library vs bookshop and actually vs currently.

objectives: Avoid common mix-ups for Arabic speakers: library vs bookshop and actually vs currently.
successCriteria: Uses library for borrowing and bookshop for buying
Uses currently for now and actually for in fact
examples: You can borrow books from the library for free.
You buy books at a bookshop.
I currently work in a bank.
It looks small, but actually it is very big.

items.prompt: Where do you borrow books for free: library or bookshop?
Which word means "now": actually or currently?

outcomes.studyNotes: In Arabic one word can mean both a place to borrow books and a place to buy books. In English there are two words. A library lends books for free. A bookshop sells books, so you buy there. Another problem is actually. Actually does not mean now. It means in fact, and we use it to correct an idea: It looks small, but actually it is big. To say now, use currently: I currently live in Dubai.

scriptedTutor.explanation: English has two words: library for borrowing and bookshop for buying. Actually means in fact. Currently means now.
hints: Is it a fact that is different, or is it now?
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Think about the meaning and try again.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. Watch these four words.

outcomes.title: Negative prefixes un-, in-, im-, dis-
outcomes.objective: Form opposites with un-, in-, im- and dis- and choose the right prefix.

misconceptions.description: Uses in- before p, m or b instead of im-

teachingSuccessCriteria: Chooses the correct negative prefix for a word
Uses im- before p, m and b

lesson.title: Prefixes that make opposites
lesson.objective: Form opposites with un-, in-, im- and dis- and choose the right prefix.

objectives: Form opposites with un-, in-, im- and dis- and choose the right prefix.
successCriteria: Chooses the correct negative prefix for a word
Uses im- before p, m and b
examples: She was unhappy about the news.
I dislike cold weather.
It is impossible to finish today.
Your answer is incorrect.

items.prompt: Add a prefix to make the opposite of "possible".
Add a prefix to make the opposite of "correct".

outcomes.studyNotes: A prefix goes at the start of a word and changes its meaning. Negative prefixes make an opposite. Un- is the most common: happy becomes unhappy. Dis- is common with verbs: like becomes dislike. In- is used with many adjectives: correct becomes incorrect. Before the letters p, m and b we use im-: possible becomes impossible. There is no simple rule for every word, so check new words in a dictionary. Do not use un- for every word.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Negative prefixes: un- (unhappy), dis- (dislike), in- (incorrect) and im- before p, m, b (impossible). Check a dictionary for new words.
hints: Look at the first letter of the word. Is it p, m or b?
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Think about the meaning and try again.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. Check unusual words in a dictionary.

outcomes.title: Adjective collocations: heavy, strong, high, deep
outcomes.objective: Choose the natural adjective (heavy, strong, high, deep) to go with a noun.
prerequisites: Knows the adjectives heavy, strong, high and deep

misconceptions.description: Translates the adjective word for word instead of using the usual partner
Uses big or very with the noun instead of the fixed adjective

teachingSuccessCriteria: Chooses the usual adjective for a noun
Rejects unnatural pairs such as strong rain

lesson.title: Natural word partners
lesson.objective: Choose the natural adjective (heavy, strong, high, deep) to go with a noun.

objectives: Choose the natural adjective (heavy, strong, high, deep) to go with a noun.
successCriteria: Chooses the usual adjective for a noun
Rejects unnatural pairs such as strong rain
examples: There was heavy rain all night.
I like strong coffee in the morning.
High prices make life hard.
Take a deep breath and relax.

outcomes.studyNotes: Some words go together naturally; these pairs are collocations. We say heavy rain, not strong rain. We say strong coffee, not heavy coffee. We say high prices, not big prices, and deep breath, not high breath. There is often no logical reason, so learn the pair together. Heavy is used for large amounts, strong for power or taste, high for numbers and levels, and deep for things that go down or feel serious. A dictionary shows common partners.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Collocations are word partners. Learn them as pairs: heavy rain, strong coffee, high prices, deep breath. The wrong partner sounds unnatural.
hints: Which adjective do people usually say with this noun?
Do not translate word for word.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Think about the meaning and try again.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. Learn adjectives together with nouns.
